title: 12. Cloud, Containers & Deployment: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service)
summary: IaaS is a cloud service model where the provider rents virtualized compute, storage, and network resources on demand, leaving the customer responsible for the operating system, middleware, runtime, and application — everything…
objectives: What does "shared responsibility" mean in IaaS, and where exactly is the line drawn?
Why is API-first provisioning considered a defining property of IaaS, and what does it enable?
Explain the IaaS billing model and why it gave rise to FinOps as a discipline.
What is a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC), and why is it foundational to IaaS networking?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** IaaS is a cloud service model where the provider rents virtualized compute, storage, and network resources on demand, leaving the customer responsible for the operating system, middleware, runtime, and application — everything above the hypervisor.
Infrastructure as a Service is the most low-level of the three classical cloud models, and it exists because renting physical hardware by the rack is economically brutal for most workloads. A mid-size company that needs 200 servers for a holiday traffic peak does not want to buy them, rack them, cable them, and pay for their power and cooling for the next three years. The cloud provider solves this by running massive data centers full of physical hosts, slicing each host into virtual machines via a hypervisor, and renting those VMs by the minute. Amazon EC2, Google Compute Engine, and Azure Virtual Machines are the canonical implementations, and together they account for the largest single slice of public cloud revenue worldwide. The customer gets the flexibility of a bare-metal machine — full root access, any operating system, any network configuration — without owning a single piece of physical hardware.

The defining property of IaaS is the shared-responsibility line drawn at the hypervisor. The provider is responsible for the physical host, the data center, power, cooling, physical network, and the hypervisor itself. The customer is responsible for everything above it: the guest operating system, patching it, hardening it, installing the runtime, configuring the firewall, deploying the application, and managing its lifecycle. This is maximum control and maximum responsibility in one bundle. Netflix, which runs one of the largest streaming workloads on Earth, made a deliberate decision in 2008 to migrate entirely off its own data centers onto AWS EC2 — not because EC2 was cheaper per compute unit, but because the capital expenditure cycle of buying servers had become a bottleneck to launching new features. Today Netflix runs hundreds of thousands of EC2 instances across multiple AWS regions, and the engineering team tunes the kernel, picks the instance types, and writes its own auto-scaling logic — exactly the kind of control IaaS affords.

The second defining property is the elasticity model. IaaS resources are exposed as APIs: a `RunInstances` call to EC2 provisions one or a thousand VMs in seconds, an `AttachVolume` call plugs in a block device, a `CreateSecurityGroup` call defines firewall rules. This API-first design is what enables auto-scaling, blue-green deploys, and chaos engineering. Netflix's Chaos Monkey, the most famous component of the Simian Army, terminates random EC2 instances in production every few minutes — and the only reason this is survivable is that the auto-scaling group replaces the instance within minutes via the same EC2 API. None of this is possible on bare metal, where a hardware failure means a ticket to a colocation vendor and a multi-day recovery. Elasticity is the operational superpower of IaaS, and it is the reason most modern architectures assume instances are disposable.

The third property is the billing model. IaaS is metered: you pay per instance-second (AWS moved from hourly to per-second billing in 2017), per GB-month of storage, per GB of egress traffic. This makes cost a first-class architectural concern in a way it never was on-premises, where a server's marginal cost was effectively zero once purchased. A poorly sized auto-scaling group can drain a million-dollar annual budget in a weekend — and the team will not notice until the bill arrives. Companies like Pinterest and Airbnb have publicly described multi-million-dollar optimizations driven by switching instance types, rightsizing, and purchasing reserved capacity. The discipline of cloud cost management (sometimes called FinOps) emerged directly as a response to IaaS metering, and it is now a board-level concern at most cloud-heavy companies.

The fourth property is the network abstraction. IaaS providers give you virtual private clouds, subnets, route tables, internet gateways, NAT gateways, and security groups — a software-defined network that mimics a physical data center but is programmable. You can spin up a three-tier VPC architecture with public subnets for load balancers, private subnets for application servers, and isolated subnets for databases in a single CloudFormation or Terraform template. Instagram's migration to AWS in 2014, which allowed them to scale from 30 million to hundreds of millions of users without buying a single server, depended heavily on this VPC model — every service ran in a private subnet with carefully scoped security group rules, reachable only through internal load balancers.

The trade-off is clear: IaaS gives you the most control and the most responsibility. You must patch your own kernels, rotate your own SSH keys, write your own autoscaling policies, and build your own deployment pipeline. Teams that want to focus only on application code typically choose PaaS or serverless, accepting less control in exchange for less operational burden. But for workloads with unusual runtime requirements — custom kernel modules, GPU-accelerated rendering, tightly tuned storage performance, or strict regulatory control over the operating system — IaaS is the only model that fits. Netflix's video encoding pipeline, which runs on custom-optimized EC2 instances with hand-tuned CPU affinities, is a textbook example: no PaaS could deliver the per-frame latency they need.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph CloudProvider["Cloud Provider Responsibility"] DC[Physical Data Center] Host[Physical Host] Net[Physical Network] HV[Hypervisor] end subgraph Customer["Customer Responsibility"] OS[Guest OS] RT[Runtime / Middleware] APP[Application] DATA[Data] end DC --> Host Host --> HV HV --> OS OS --> RT RT --> APP APP --> DATA API[Provisioning API
RunInstances / AttachVolume] -.-> HV API2[Billing / Metering] -.-> HV ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +---------------------------------------------+ | Cloud Provider (AWS / GCP / Azure) | | | | +-------+ +-------+ +-------+ | | | Host1 | | Host2 | | Host3 | | | | HV | | HV | | HV | | | +-------+ +-------+ +-------+ | | | | | | | | +--------+-----------+----------+ | | | | Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) | | | | | +------------------------+ | | | | | | Subnet (private) | | | | | | | +------+ +------+ | | | | | | | | VM A | | VM B | | | | | | | | | OS | | OS | | | | | | | | | App | | App | | | | | | | | +------+ +------+ | | | | | | +------------------------+ | | | | +-------------------------------+ | | | | | v | | +----------+ +-----------+ | | | EBS vol | | S3 / obj | | | | (block) | | storage | | | +----------+ +-----------+ | | | +---------------------------------------------+ ^ | RunInstances / AttachVolume / CreateSG | +----------------+ | Customer API | <-- Terraform / CloudFormation / boto3 +----------------+ ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The cloud provider operates physical hosts in a data center and runs a hypervisor on each to slice them into virtual machines. The customer never touches the hardware. 2. The customer calls the provider's API (via Terraform, CloudFormation, or boto3) to launch VMs into a virtual private cloud, attach block storage volumes, and define security group rules. 3. The hypervisor boots the guest operating system from a chosen AMI or image; from that moment the customer is fully responsible for OS patching, runtime installation, application deployment, and data management. 4. Metering kicks in: every instance-second, GB-month of storage, and GB of egress is recorded and billed, making cost a function of architecture rather than procurement.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- A minimal mock of EC2/GCE/Azure-VM primitives.
- Mimic an ASG: detect terminated, relaunch to maintain desired count.
- Iaas_provisioning.py - runnable mock of IaaS provisioning primitives
- Models: launch instances, attach EBS volumes, configure security groups,
- Tag for billing, and simulate autoscaling replacement.
- Simulate Chaos Monkey killing one instance
- ASG restores desired count

**Defines:** `Instance`, `Volume`, `SecurityGroup`, `IaaSCloud`

```python
# iaas_provisioning.py - runnable mock of IaaS provisioning primitives
# Models: launch instances, attach EBS volumes, configure security groups,
# tag for billing, and simulate autoscaling replacement.
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List, Dict
import uuid, time, random

@dataclass
class Instance:
    instance_id: str
    instance_type: str
    ami: str
    private_ip: str
    state: str = "pending"           # pending -> running -> stopped -> terminated
    tags: Dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)
    attached_volumes: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)

@dataclass
class Volume:
    volume_id: str
    size_gb: int
    volume_type: str
    attached_to: str = None          # instance_id or None

class SecurityGroup:
    def __init__(self, name: str, vpc_id: str):
        self.group_id = "sg-" + uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
        self.name = name
        self.vpc_id = vpc_id
        self.ingress: List[Dict] = []   # list of {port, cidr, proto}
    def allow(self, port: int, cidr: str, proto: str = "tcp"):
        self.ingress.append({"port": port, "cidr": cidr, "proto": proto})
        print(f"  SG[{self.name}] ingress {proto}/{port} from {cidr}")

class IaaSCloud:
    """A minimal mock of EC2/GCE/Azure-VM primitives."""
    def __init__(self, region: str):
        self.region = region
        self.instances: Dict[str, Instance] = {}
        self.volumes: Dict[str, Volume] = {}
        self.sgs: Dict[str, SecurityGroup] = {}

    def run_instances(self, count: int, itype: str = "m5.xlarge",
                      ami: str = "ami-0abcdef", sg: SecurityGroup = None,
                      tags: Dict[str, str] = None) -> List[Instance]:
        launched = []
        for _ in range(count):
            iid = "i-" + uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
            ip = f"10.0.{random.randint(0,255)}.{random.randint(2,254)}"
            inst = Instance(iid, itype, ami, ip, tags=tags or {})
            self.instances[iid] = inst
            # simulate boot time
            time.sleep(0.05)
            inst.state = "running"
            launched.append(inst)
            print(f"[run_instances] launched {iid} ({itype}) @ {ip}  tags={inst.tags}")
        return launched

    def create_volume(self, size_gb: int, vtype: str = "gp3") -> Volume:
        vid = "vol-" + uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
        vol = Volume(vid, size_gb, vtype)
        self.volumes[vid] = vol
        print(f"[create_volume] {vid} {size_gb}GB {vtype}")
        return vol

    def attach_volume(self, vol: Volume, inst: Instance):
        vol.attached_to = inst.instance_id
        inst.attached_volumes.append(vol.volume_id)
        print(f"[attach_volume] {vol.volume_id} -> {inst.instance_id}")

    def terminate(self, iid: str):
        if iid in self.instances:
            self.instances[iid].state = "terminated"
            print(f"[terminate] {iid} terminated")
            # detach volumes
            for vid in list(self.instances[iid].attached_volumes):
                self.volumes[vid].attached_to = None

    def autoscale_replacement(self, sg: SecurityGroup, ami: str,
                              desired: int, tag_key: str, tag_val: str):
        """Mimic an ASG: detect terminated, relaunch to maintain desired count."""
        alive = [i for i in self.instances.values()
                 if i.tags.get(tag_key) == tag_val and i.state == "running"]
        missing = desired - len(alive)
        if missing > 0:
            print(f"[autoscale] {missing} instance(s) short, launching replacements...")
            self.run_instances(missing, itype="m5.xlarge", ami=ami, sg=sg,
                               tags={tag_key: tag_val, "managed_by": "asg"})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cloud = IaaSCloud(region="us-east-1")
    sg = SecurityGroup("web-sg", vpc_id="vpc-1")
    sg.allow(443, "0.0.0.0/0")
    sg.allow(22, "10.0.0.0/8")

    web = cloud.run_instances(3, itype="m5.xlarge", ami="ami-0abcdef",
                              sg=sg, tags={"role": "web", "env": "prod"})
    for inst in web:
        v = cloud.create_volume(100)
        cloud.attach_volume(v, inst)

    # Simulate Chaos Monkey killing one instance
    victim = web[0].instance_id
    cloud.terminate(victim)

    # ASG restores desired count
    cloud.autoscale_replacement(sg, "ami-0abcdef", desired=3,
                                tag_key="role", tag_val="web")
    print(f"final fleet: {len([i for i in cloud.instances.values() if i.state=='running'])} running")
```
